lutheran.means_of_grace:
Lutherans teach that God gives forgiveness, life and faith through means: the gospel proclaimed in the Word and in the sacraments of Baptism and the Lord's Supper. Many also include absolution, the declaration of forgiveness. Through these ordinary, visible things the Holy Spirit works to create and to sustain faith.

Lutherans stress that these means are God's own actions and promises, and not human efforts to reach him. This is why Word and sacrament stand at the center of congregational life and why Lutherans look to them for assurance: the promise of forgiveness is spoken to you, and given to you in water, bread and wine. It differs from views in which grace comes only through inward experience, and from views in which grace is thought to work automatically.
lutheran.sola_scriptura:
Lutherans hold that Scripture alone is the norm for teaching and life in the church: it is the source and standard by which all doctrine is judged. The Lutheran Confessions, gathered in the Book of Concord, are honored as a faithful exposition of what Scripture teaches, but they are subject to Scripture and not above it.

This does not mean that Lutherans reject the church's earlier tradition. They keep the ancient creeds, the church's liturgy and much of its worship, and they value the teachers of the early church. What they insist is that tradition serves Scripture and can be corrected by it. This differs from traditions that treat tradition as a second and equal source of authority, and Lutherans generally explain the difference carefully.
lutheran.infant_baptism:
Lutherans baptize infants, and teach that Baptism is God's action in which he washes away sin, gives new birth by the Holy Spirit and unites the child to Christ. It is not a human decision but a gift, and it is given to children on the ground of God's promise, which is meant for them as much as for adults.

Faith is understood as itself a gift of the Holy Spirit, which God can work in a child. The child is then taught the faith at home and in church as the baptized person grows. Lutherans consider a person's baptism to remain valid throughout life, and daily repentance a return to it. They differ from churches that baptize only those who can make their own profession of faith, and they explain that Baptism depends on God's promise, not on the person's understanding.
lutheran.confirmation:
In Lutheran churches confirmation is not regarded as a sacrament. It is a rite that follows a period of instruction in the faith, usually based on Luther's Small Catechism, at which baptized young people publicly affirm the faith into which they were baptized and, in many churches, are admitted to receive the Lord's Supper.

The rite marks the completion of a period of basic teaching, and it does not add anything to Baptism. The age and the way it is done differ by church and region, with some churches admitting younger children to communion before confirmation. Lutherans see it as a natural moment for the young person to take on their own baptismal faith and to be blessed with prayer and the laying on of hands.
lutheran.real_presence:
Lutherans teach the real presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper: the true body and blood of Christ are present in, with and under the bread and wine, and all who receive them receive Christ's body and blood, some to their blessing and some, if they do not believe, to their judgment. This is often called the sacramental union.

Lutherans hold this on the basis of Jesus' words, this is my body, this is my blood, taken as they stand. They do not teach that the bread and wine cease to be bread and wine, as in transubstantiation, and they do not treat the meal as a memorial only. The way Christ is present is a mystery which they receive in faith, and they trust his promise that the meal gives forgiveness of sins, life and salvation.
lutheran.eucharistic_sacrifice:
Lutherans teach that the Lord's Supper is a gift that God gives to us, and not a sacrifice which the church offers to God to obtain forgiveness. Christ offered himself once for all on the cross, and nothing can be added to it. The Supper delivers the benefits of that sacrifice to those who receive it.

Lutherans do speak of a sacrifice of praise: the church responds to the gift with thanksgiving, prayer, and lives offered to God. In this sense worship includes sacrifice, but it is a response and not an attempt to earn favor. This is one of the ways Lutherans distinguish their understanding from teaching of the Mass as a sacrifice, and they are careful to describe the difference between receiving a gift and offering one.
lutheran.closed_communion:
Some Lutheran churches, including the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod and the Wisconsin Evangelical Lutheran Synod, practice closed communion, also called altar fellowship. Communion is given to those who are members of the congregation or of a church in agreement with it in doctrine, after instruction and examination.

The reasons given are the words of the apostle Paul about receiving the Supper worthily, and the belief that sharing the Supper expresses agreement in the faith. Pastors are also responsible for the spiritual care of those they commune. It is not intended as a judgment on other Christians' faith. Other Lutheran bodies, such as the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America, practice a more open communion, welcoming baptized Christians of other churches.
lutheran.liturgy:
Lutherans understand the main Sunday service as the Divine Service, in which God serves his people by giving them his Word and sacrament, and the people respond with prayer, praise and thanksgiving. The service follows the historic pattern of the western church: confession and absolution, the Kyrie and hymn of praise, readings, the creed, the sermon, the prayers and the Lord's Supper.

Lutherans kept the liturgy at the Reformation, purified of what they considered unbiblical, because they regard it as a good way to teach and to carry the gospel. The degree of formality varies widely. Some congregations follow a full traditional liturgy, others use contemporary music and simplified forms, but most keep the core of Word and sacrament as the center of worship.
lutheran.sign_of_the_cross:
Lutherans use the sign of the cross as a reminder of Baptism and of Christ's cross. Luther's Small Catechism directs that it be made in the morning and evening prayers, and it is commonly used in the liturgy at the invocation of the Trinity, at the blessing and at the absolution, and in the baptism service.

It is not commanded by Scripture and is not required, so its use is a matter of Christian freedom, and some Lutherans use it often while others seldom. It is understood as a confession of faith and of trust in Christ, and as a way to remember that one belongs to him. It is not thought to have power in itself, and Lutherans stress that it points to Christ and his promise.
lutheran.perpetual_virginity:
Lutheran teaching honors Mary as the mother of the Lord and, in the Smalcald Articles of the Lutheran Confessions, calls her the ever-virgin. Martin Luther himself held that Mary remained a virgin throughout her life, and this view was common among the early Lutheran teachers.

Modern Lutherans differ on the point. Some continue to hold the traditional view as part of their heritage. Others regard it as a pious opinion that Scripture neither commands nor forbids, and so leave it a matter of freedom. What all Lutherans confess is the virgin birth of Jesus and Mary's honored place in the story of salvation. They do not teach prayer to Mary, and they place the emphasis on what her story shows about Christ.
